section.heading: 3.1. Derivatives of Polynomials and Exponential Functions
section.paragraph: In this section we learn how to differentiate constant functions, power functions, polynomials, and exponential functions.
section.heading: Constant Functions
section.paragraph: Let’s start with the simplest of all functions, the constant function $$f(x) = c$$ . The graph of this function is the horizontal line $$y = c$$ , which has slope $$0$$ , so we must have $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ . (See Figure 1.) A formal proof, from the definition of a derivative, is also easy:
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{c - c}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}0 = 0$$

figure.caption: The graph of $$f(x) = c$$ is the line $$y = c$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ .

section.heading: Power Functions
section.paragraph: We next look at the functions $$f(x) = x^{n}$$ , where $$n$$ is a positive integer. If $$n = 1$$ , the graph of $$f(x) = x$$ is the line $$y = x$$ , which has slope $$1$$ . (See Figure 2.) So
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x) = 1$$

Comparing the equations in (1), (2), and (3), we see a pattern emerging. It seems to be a reasonable guess that, when $$n$$ is a positive integer, $$\left( {d \slash dx} \right)\left( x^{n} \right) = nx^{n - 1}$$ . This turns out to be true. We prove it in two ways; the second proof uses the Binomial Theorem.

section.heading: Second Proof
section.paragraph: $$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {x + h} \right)^{n} - x^{n}}{h}$$
In finding the derivative of $$x^{4}$$ we had to expand $$\left( {x + h} \right)^{4}$$ . Here we need to expand $$\left( {x + h} \right)^{n}$$ and we use the Binomial Theorem to do so:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow o}\frac{\left\lbrack {x^{n} + nx^{n - 1}h + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}x^{n - 2}h^{2} + \cdots + nxh^{n - 1} + h^{n}} \right\rbrack - x^{n}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{nx^{n - 1}h + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}x^{n - 2}h^{2} + \cdots + nxh^{n - 1} + h^{n}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left\lbrack {nx^{n - 1} + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}x^{n - 2}h + \cdots + nxh^{n - 2} + h^{n - 1}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {nx^{n - 1}}} \end{array}$$
because every term except the first has $$h$$ as a factor and therefore approaches $$0$$ .
The Binomial Theorem is given on A Preview of Calculus .
We illustrate the Power Rule using various notations in Example 1.
What about power functions with negative integer exponents? In Exercise 69 we ask you to verify from the definition of a derivative that
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$
We can rewrite this equation as
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{- 1})} = \left( {- 1} \right)x^{- 2}$$
and so the Power Rule is true when $$n = - 1$$ . In fact, we will show in the next section [Exercise 3.2.66(c)] that it holds for all negative integers.
What if the exponent is a fraction? In Example 2.8.3 we found that
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\sqrt{x} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$$
which can be written as
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{(x^{1 \slash 2})} = \frac{1}{2}x^{- 1 \slash 2}$$
This shows that the Power Rule is true even when the exponent is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . In fact, we will show in Section 3.6 that it is true for all real exponents $$n$$ .

section.paragraph: The Power Rule enables us to find tangent lines without having to resort to the definition of a derivative. It also enables us to find normal lines. The normal line to a curve $$C$$ at a point $$P$$ is the line through $$P$$ that is perpendicular to the tangent line at $$P$$ . (In the study of optics, the Law of Reflection involves the angle between a light ray and the normal line to a lens.)

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find equations of the tangent line and normal line to the curve $$y = x\sqrt{x}$$ at the point $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ . Illustrate by graphing the curve and these lines.
Solution The derivative of $$f(x) = x\sqrt{x} = xx^{1 \slash 2} = x^{3 \slash 2}$$ is
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{3}{2}x^{(3 \slash 2) - 1} = \frac{3}{2}x^{1 \slash 2} = \frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}$$
So the slope of the tangent line at $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ is $$f^{\prime}(1) = \frac{3}{2}$$ . Therefore an equation of the tangent line is
$$y - 1 = \frac{3}{2}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$

section.heading: New Derivatives from Old
section.paragraph: When new functions are formed from old functions by addition, subtraction, or multiplication by a constant, their derivatives can be calculated in terms of derivatives of the old functions. In particular, the following formula says that the derivative of a constant times a function is the constant times the derivative of the function.

note.title: The Constant Multiple Rule
note.heading: The Constant Multiple Rule
note.paragraph: If $$c$$ is a constant and $$f$$ is a differentiable function, then

The next rule tells us that the derivative of a sum (or difference) of functions is the sum (or difference) of the derivatives.

note.title: The Sum and Difference Rules
note.heading: The Sum and Difference Rules
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ and $$g$$ are both differentiable, then

section.paragraph: Using prime notation, we can write the Sum and Difference Rules as
$$\begin{matrix} {(f + g)^{\prime} = f^{\prime} + g^{\prime}} \\ {(f - g)^{\prime} = f^{\prime} - g^{\prime}} \end{matrix}$$

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: To prove the Sum Rule, we let $$F(x) = f(x) + g(x)$$ . Then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{F^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{F\left( {x + h} \right) - F(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left\lbrack {f\left( {x + h} \right) + g\left( {x + h} \right)} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {f(x) + g(x)} \right\rbrack}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left\lbrack {\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} + \frac{g\left( {x + h} \right) - g(x)}{h}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} + \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{g\left( {x + h} \right) - g(x)}{h}{ ({by Limit Law 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {f^{\prime}(x) + g^{\prime}(x)}} \end{array}$$
To prove the Difference Rule, we write $$f - g$$ as $$f + ( - 1)g$$ and apply the Sum Rule and the Constant Multiple Rule.

section.paragraph: The Sum Rule can be extended to the sum of any number of functions. For instance, using this theorem twice, we get
$$\left( {f + g + h} \right)^{\prime} = \left\lbrack {\left( {f + g} \right) + h} \right\rbrack^{\prime} = \left( {f + g} \right)^{\prime} + h^{\prime} = f^{\prime} + g^{\prime} + h^{\prime}$$
The Constant Multiple Rule, the Sum Rule, and the Difference Rule can be combined with the Power Rule to differentiate any polynomial, as the following three examples demonstrate.

Thus $$dy \slash dx = 0$$ if $$x = 0$$ or $$x^{2} - 3 = 0$$ , that is, $$x = \pm \sqrt{3^{}}$$ . So the given curve has horizontal tangents when $$x = 0$$ , $$\sqrt{3^{}}$$ , and $$- \sqrt{3^{}}$$ . example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: The equation of motion of a particle is $$s = 2t^{3} - 5t^{2} + 3t + 4$$ , where $$s$$ is measured in centimeters and $$t$$ in seconds. Find the acceleration as a function of time. What is the acceleration after $$2$$ seconds?
Solution The velocity and acceleration are
$$\begin{array}{rll} {\upsilon(t)} & = & {\frac{ds}{dt} = 6t^{2} - 10t + 3} \\ {a(t)} & = & {\frac{d\upsilon}{dt} = 12t - 10} \end{array}$$
The acceleration after $$2$$ seconds is $$a(2) = 14{cm} \slash s^{2}$$ .

section.heading: Exponential Functions
section.paragraph: Let’s try to compute the derivative of the exponential function $$f(x) = b^{ x}$$ using the definition of a derivative:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{ x + h} - b^{ x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{ x}b^{ h} - b^{ x}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{ x}{({b^{ h} - 1})}}{h}}} \end{array}$$
The factor $$b^{ x}$$ doesn’t depend on $$h$$ , so we can take it in front of the limit:
$$f^{\prime}(x) = b^{ x}\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{ h} - 1}{h}$$
Notice that the limit is the value of the derivative of $$f$$ at $$0$$ , that is,
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{b^{ h} - 1}{h} = f^{\prime}(0)$$
Therefore we have shown that if the exponential function $$f(x) = b^{ x}$$ is differentiable at $$0$$ , then it is differentiable everywhere and
$$f^{\prime}(x) = f^{\prime}(0)b^{ x}$$
This equation says that the rate of change of any exponential function is proportional to the function itself. (The slope is proportional to the height.)

Numerical evidence for the existence of $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ is given in the table below for the cases $$b = 2$$ and $$b = 3$$ . (Values are stated correct to live decimal places.) It can be proved that the limits exist and

$$\begin{matrix} { \text{for} b} & = & {2,} & {f^{\prime}(0)} & = & {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{2^{h} - 1}{h} \approx 0.693} \\ { \text{for} b} & = & {3,} & {f^{\prime}(0)} & = & {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3^{h} - 1}{h} \approx 1.099} \end{matrix}$$
Thus, from Equation 4 we have
$${\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 2^{ x} \right) \approx (0.693)2^{ x}}{ \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( 3^{x} \right) \approx (1.099)3^{x}}$$

Of all possible choices for the base $$b$$ in Equation 4, the simplest differentiation formula occurs when $$f^{\prime}(0) = 1$$ . In view of the estimates of $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ for $$b = 2$$ and $$b = 3$$ , it seems reasonable that there is a number $$b$$ between $$2$$ and $$3$$ for which $$f^{\prime}(0) = 1$$ . It is traditional to denote this value by the letter $$e$$ . (In fact, that is how we introduced $$e$$ in Section 1.4.) Thus we have the following definition.

section.paragraph: Thus the exponential function $$f(x) = e^{ x}$$ has the property that it is its own derivative. The geometrical significance of this fact is that the slope of a tangent line to the curve $$y = e^{ x}$$ at the point $$\left. \left( x,e^{ x} \right. \right)$$ is equal to the $$y$$ -coordinate of the point (see Figure 7).

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = e^{ x} - x$$ , find $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$f^{''}$$ . Compare the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ .
Solution Using the Difference Rule, we have
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {e^{ x} - x} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(x) = e^{ x} - 1$$
In Section 2.8 we defined the second derivative as the derivative of $$f^{\prime}$$ , so
$$f^{''}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {e^{ x} - 1} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( e^{ x} \right) - \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}(1) = e^{ x}$$

The function $$f$$ and its derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ are graphed in Figure 8. Notice that $$f$$ has a horizontal tangent when $$x = 0$$ ; this corresponds to the fact that $$f^{\prime}(0) = 0$$ . Notice also that, for $$x > 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive and $$f$$ is increasing. When $$x < 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative and $$f$$ is decreasing.

section.heading: Applied Project Building a Better Roller Coaster
section.paragraph: Suppose you are asked to design the first ascent and drop for a new roller coaster. By studying photographs of your favorite coasters, you decide to make the slope of the ascent $$0.8$$ and the slope of the drop $$- 1.6$$ . You decide to connect these two straight stretches $$y = L_{1}(x)$$ and $$y = L_{2}(x)$$ with part of a parabola $$y = f(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c$$ , where $$x$$ and $$f(x)$$ are measured in feet. For the track to be smooth there can’t be abrupt changes in direction, so you want the linear segments $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ to be tangent to the parabola at the transition points $$P$$ and $$Q$$ . (See the figure.) To simplify the equations, you decide to place the origin at $$P$$ .

The tangent line labeled L_1 with a positive slope is drawn on the left half of the parabola, intersecting it at a labeled point P. Another tangent line labeled L_2 with a negative slope is drawn on the right half of the parabola, intersecting it at a labeled point Q. The photo shows a roller coaster sliding down from a high point.

list.item: Suppose the horizontal distance between $$P$$ and $$Q$$ is $$100$$ ft. Write equations in $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ that will ensure that the track is smooth at the transition points. Solve the equations in part (a) for $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ to find a formula for $$f(x)$$ . Plot $$L_{1}$$ , $$f$$ , and $$L_{2}$$ to verify graphically that the transitions are smooth.
